demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Maladaptive Strategies.value: perform mental rituals to prevent bad things from happening again
I remind myself it could have been worse
I dwell on what I have done wrong

Threat.value: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong
I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people

Memory.value: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory
I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns
When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.

Negative Appraisals.value: Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation
I feel isolated and set apart from others
The person I have become is unrecognisable to me

issues.item: Self-Harm Distraction: I hurt myself physically to stop thinking about the event
issues.explanation: Self-harm as a coping strategy is not impossible, but in this profile it is the only markedly high-risk/impulsive strategy and is poorly supported by the rest of the selected nodes. The other strategies are comparatively cognitive/obsessional (mental rituals, downward comparison), and the threat/memory/appraisal items do not show the broader dysregulation, dissociation, or severe affective overload that would make this combination clinically cohesive.

issues.item: Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event
issues.explanation: Pain recall implies the patient was physically injured in the traumatic event. That is hard to reconcile with the trauma type 'accidentally caused serious injury to another' unless she was also injured, which is not otherwise reflected anywhere in the profile. The rest of the memory items emphasize fragmented retrieval and sensory reliving, but not a personally injured trauma narrative.

vignette: Linda is a 47-year-old African-American architect who has been struggling with symptoms following an incident at work where she accidentally caused serious injury to another person. The traumatic event left her feeling overwhelmed and isolated from her colleagues and friends. Linda’s self-blame and difficulty in concentrating on tasks have significantly impacted her ability to perform effectively in her profession. The day of the accident was a blur, but specific details stand out vividly in her memory. She recalls the metallic taste of blood mixed with fear that she can still taste when intrusive memories resurface. The auditory recall is equally vivid; she often hears the sounds of alarms and screaming in her head, reminiscent of that fateful day. When Linda tries to deliberately recall what happened, it becomes difficult for her to access these memories, further complicating her emotional processing. Linda’s sense of self has been profoundly altered by this event. She feels unrecognisable to herself, which leads to feelings of isolation and a belief that she is set apart from others. These negative appraisals have fueled her maladaptive strategies. Linda engages in mental rituals, believing that if she performs these actions meticulously, she can prevent similar bad things from happening again. This magical prevention helps her cope with the overwhelming self-blame and ruminations about what she has done wrong. The constant self-comparisons to others who she believes would not have gotten into this situation exacerbate her sense of isolation and unrecognisability. She often reminds herself that it could have been worse, but this does little to alleviate her distress. Linda’s memories are fragmented and hard to access deliberately, which further complicates her attempts at healing. Linda's intrusive memories often trigger false alarms where she reacts as if she is in immediate danger, even when there is no real threat present. These false alarms make it difficult for her to concentrate on her work, leading to mistakes that exacerbate her feelings of incompetence and self-blame. The sounds around her can be jarring, making her jump or startle at ordinary noises, which reinforces the sense of danger she feels. Over time, these experiences have formed a cycle where Linda’s maladaptive strategies worsen both her memory issues and negative appraisals. She performs mental rituals to manage her anxiety, but this only serves to reinforce the notion that she is in constant danger. Her isolation deepens as she withdraws from social interactions due to her fear of being judged or misunderstood. Linda's work environment has become a source of significant distress. The sounds and sights associated with construction sites trigger intense reactions for her. She often finds herself staring blankly at blueprints, unable to focus on the details that once came easily to her. This struggle at work is not only affecting her performance but also her relationships with colleagues. The constant vigilance and self-blame have taken a toll on Linda's life. Her marriage has felt strained as she retreats into herself, struggling to communicate effectively about what she is experiencing. The cumulative effect of these symptoms led her to finally seek help after a particularly distressing episode at work, where she froze during an important presentation. Linda is now seeking therapy, hoping to regain control over her life and find ways to cope with the overwhelming feelings that have dominated her since the accident. She fears being unable to return to her job effectively or losing the connections that once brought her joy. Linda’s most profound hope is to feel like herself again, to understand why this happened, and to move past it. The cycle of negative appraisals, maladaptive strategies, memory issues, and heightened threat responses has created a complex web of distress for Linda. Her journey towards recovery will involve breaking down these connections, understanding the origins of her fears, and developing more adaptive coping mechanisms to navigate through this challenging period.
